newsitem.title: GERMANY: Mercedes-Benz boss tipped to resign.
newsitem.headline: Mercedes-Benz boss tipped to resign.

text.p: Mercedes-Benz AG chairman Helmut Werner, the architect of the biggest shift in strategy in the car maker's history, seemed closer to resigning on Thursday as two respected newspapers said he was about to quit.

Werner, who had opposed a massive restructuring at parent Daimler-Benz AG, was likely to announce his departure as early as next week, frustrated that Mercedes would no longer remain an independent company, the papers said.

Two dailies, the Stuttgarter Zeitung and the Boersen-Zeitung, said the respected Mercedes boss was not able to strike a compromise with Daimler-Benz chairman Juergen Schrempp over the future shape of Daimler-Benz, Germany's largest company.
A Daimler-Benz spokesman declined to comment on the reports.

The articles carried special urgency with a four-man presidium of Daimler executives meeting on Thursday afternoon to discuss the reorganisation plans and prepare a recommendation for a supervisory board meeeting on January 23 that is to approve the final reorganisation strategy.
The German press for weeks has carried stories of a power struggle between Werner and Schrempp over the future of Mercedes -- reports both men have downplayed saying they are friends.
At issue is the future of Mercedes, one of the world's most profitable car companies.
Under the Daimler plan, Mercedes would cease to be a seperate legal entity and would become part of Daimler-Benz, represented by three officials on the Daimler board, company officials said.
The two other major Daimler units, Diamler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA) and Debis AG, would remain separate legal companies.

Daimler officials have downplayed reports of a power struggle between Schrempp and Werner, saying the restructuring plan reflected an acknowledgement that Mercedes will remain the biggest share of Daimler's business for the foreseeable future.
The restructuring is designed to speed decision making at the group and cut overheads, saving the company millions of marks a year, according to some reports.
Werner took over Mercedes in 1993 when it was losing money and swiftly directed the company into a wide range of new models including the hot-selling SLK sports car and the small A-Class city car.
